claim: At this storm’s peak, 837 fewer vacant taxis than expected.
method: A storm-day shortfall, measured against the usual level
analysis: At 09:30, there are 1,473 taxis versus 2,309.6 expected: 837 fewer (−36.2%). At 08:30, the 258 cells with no rain in the preceding half-hour already have 11.6% fewer than expected.
decision: The rain footprint alone misses part of the supply gap. A useful warning system must look beyond the square under the cloud.
next_question: Does this pattern persist across years, after usual place and time differences are controlled?

claim: Heavy rain is associated with 12.9% fewer vacant taxis.
analysis: Light, moderate and heavy rain correspond to 7.7%, 10.8% and 12.9% fewer vacant taxis. Heavy rain still has a −5.7% local-share association after the citywide comparison.
decision: Rain is linked to both a wider supply drop and extra local losses. Focusing only on the wet square would miss the wider part.
next_question: Which places and times have the largest losses?

claim: The central-area percentage loss is about twice as large.
analysis: The central-area contrast is −24.2% versus −11.9% outside. Weekday rush periods show −18.1% versus −11.3% at other times.
decision: Rain plans should give extra attention to central coverage and weekday peaks. Next, translate percentages into the number of taxis involved.
next_question: Does the largest percentage loss also mean the most taxis lost?

claim: Changi loses more taxis; Bayfront loses a larger fraction.
analysis: Changi T3: 7.08 of 83.37 taxis (−8.50%). Marina Bay Sands: 4.76 of 13.08 (−36.42%). The airport loses more taxis; Bayfront loses a larger fraction.
decision: Use taxi counts to size a staging trial and percentages to judge local severity. The two rankings answer different planning questions.
next_question: When should a response start, and how long does the gap remain?

claim: The deepest average gap is in the first hour.
analysis: Availability is 5.3% lower at onset and 5.6% lower 30 minutes later. The estimate narrows to −1.3% at +120 minutes; from +150 minutes, all later intervals include zero.
decision: The deepest average gap comes early. Waiting until after rain starts leaves little time for a driver to reposition.
next_question: Is there any useful signal before local rain begins?

claim: Supply is already lower before local rain arrives.
method: Test nearby rain and forecasts while the cell stays dry
analysis: Rain >2.5 mm/h 2–5 km away is associated with 7.3% fewer vacant taxis in a still-dry cell. An issued thundery forecast corresponds to −5.1%, or −3.7% with neighbouring rain controlled.
decision: Nearby rain and issued forecasts are plausible early signals. Their predictive value still needs a direct with/without-weather test.
next_question: Does the response depend more on intensity, spell length, or time since rain?

claim: The supply gap is larger during long heavy-rain spells.
analysis: The intensity curve reaches −9.7% at only 1 mm/h. Heavy spells deepen from −11.4% in the first half-hour to −18.0% beyond two hours. The saved 30–60-minute after-rain bin is −5.3%.
decision: Rain planning needs spell length as well as intensity. An extreme-intensity trigger alone would miss gaps already present in lighter rain.
next_question: When rain covers the island, can another area reliably supply spare taxis?

claim: Island-wide rain leaves few clear gainers to draw taxis from.
method: Compare local shares during island-wide rain
analysis: 329 of 374 cells have clearly fewer vacant taxis; only 3 clearly gain. Several eastern and northern cells gain citywide share while their actual taxi counts still fall.
decision: A relative gainer is not automatically a donor area. A repositioning plan must check the current surplus before drawing taxis from it.
next_question: Can a model identify the next low-supply cells accurately enough to act?

claim: Taxi information improves alerts. Weather barely changes them.
method: Forecast the same targets with and without weather
analysis: At 30 minutes, 54.23% of LightGBM alerts are correct versus 47.18% for persistence. At 60 minutes: 51.95% versus 43.99%. Weather gives 54.20% and 51.88%.
decision: The model improves alert ranking, but adding the tested weather inputs barely changes it. The next test checks whether a different target or scale changes that conclusion.
next_question: Is the small weather gain just a consequence of the 1 km target or its label?

claim: Changing the grid and label still adds little forecast skill.
method: Registered secondary tests across targets and scales
analysis: 0 of 36 comparisons reaches the +0.0100 materiality bar. The largest gain is +0.0024; larger grids and the noise-aware label do not rescue the tested weather features.
decision: The weak increment is not confined to one sparse-cell definition. Use the stronger taxi-information model while testing any new weather approach separately.
next_question: Even with better ranking, how often do alerts arrive before a shortfall starts?

claim: Most shortfalls still receive no advance warning.
method: Measure warning before each low-supply run
analysis: Only 6.65% of runs receive advance warning at 30 minutes and 13.79% at 60. About 83% are never alerted under this workload.
decision: Correct alerts are not enough: most shortfalls lack advance warning. This limits how much proactive repositioning the current system can support.
next_question: Could weather work better for regional shortfalls specifically during storms?

claim: Regional storm forecasts show a small, unconfirmed weather gain.
method: Test frozen regional models on separate holdouts
analysis: October 2026 gives +0.0238, but only 2 storms versus 8 required. In 2019, 49 storms give +0.0087 [0.0008, 0.0171], below +0.02.
decision: There is small positive regional weather information, but no adequately powered confirmation of a material gain. October’s promising point estimate is not confirmation.
next_question: Does weather help a different decision: planning the coming day at 09:00?

claim: Weather helps daily planning in the flexible model.
method: Predict daily exposure using information available by 09:00
analysis: The flexible model lowers deviance by 6.3% on the issue-time label and 10.1% retrospectively. The linear model is flat or worse: −4.5% on issue-time.
decision: Weather helps the coarser daily-planning task in the flexible model. That supports testing advance staffing/staging schedules, rather than claiming better immediate cell alerts.
next_question: Which areas and time bands should a planning trial focus on?

claim: The planning window depends on both place and time.
method: Aggregate forecast-conditioned gaps by place and time
analysis: Changi: roughly 25–33 fewer taxis early in the day. Bukit Merah: roughly 21–25 fewer in evening/night periods. Central-area gaps have a different daily pattern.
decision: A single island-wide incentive window would miss these differences. A planning trial should specify both an area and a time band.
next_question: How much targeting precision survives actual staging and supply constraints?

analysis: Unconstrained ranking reaches 51.47% precision. Eligibility/staging gives 48.05%; the risk-weighted allocation gives 44.16%, versus 31.01% for the original policy.
decision: Use risk weighting for a staging pilot, with live donor checks and travel limits. Operational feasibility costs targeting precision; the final plan still needs an intervention trial.
next_question: Recommendation: use live supply for dispatch and the morning forecast for a targeted planning trial.
